title: Watching Single Motors and Filaments Move
endLine: Watch purified parts under a microscope to see what averages hide.

scenes.tts: How do you watch one motor work when many act together? Inside a cell, crowded filaments and motors blur into one average. Pull purified parts into a glass microscope chamber instead.
scenes.caption: How do you watch one motor work when many act together? Inside a cell, crowded filaments and motors blur into one average. Pull purified parts into a glass microscope chamber instead.
scenes.visual: Open immediately on a crowded schematic cell interior with dozens of glowing filaments and small motor icons moving out of sync in a blur while the opening question appears as a short label ('Watch one motor?'). The blur smooths into one flat average bar, then clears and zooms into our carried world: a shallow dark glass microscope chamber filling most of the frame height, with a clean glass floor along the bottom, slow drifting background specks, and a single glowing filament and one simple two-footed motor (all schematic, no molecular structures).
scenes.narration: How do you watch one motor work when many act together? Inside a cell, crowded filaments and motors blur into one average. Pull purified parts into a glass microscope chamber instead.

scenes.tts: Working outside the cell, in vitro, lets you choose each ingredient. Add purified polar tracks, actin or microtubules, each with two distinct ends. Use fluorescence or dark-field microscopy so single tracks shine in the dark. Add A T P, and watch motion begin.
scenes.caption: Working outside the cell, in vitro, lets you choose each ingredient. Add purified polar tracks, actin or microtubules, each with two distinct ends. Use fluorescence or dark-field microscopy so single tracks shine in the dark. Add ATP, and watch motion begin.
scenes.visual: Stay inside the same dark glass microscope chamber (schematic). Label 'In vitro' briefly at top. Two simple polar tracks glide into place: an actin rod marked with barbed (+) and pointed (-) ends, and a hollow microtubule tube marked with plus (+) and minus (-) ends. A soft light sweep switches them into bright fluorescent glow against the dark fluid. Small glowing ATP dots drift in from the side as motion starts along the tracks.
scenes.narration: Working outside the cell, in vitro, lets you choose each ingredient. Add purified polar tracks, actin or microtubules, each with two distinct ends. Use fluorescence or dark-field microscopy so single tracks shine in the dark. Add ATP, and watch motion begin.

scenes.tts: On its track, each motor foot grips, swings while gripping, lets go, and re-cocks. One step's work cannot exceed the energy of one A T P. Force times step is at most about eighty to one hundred piconewton-nanometres. Watching purified parts one by one reveals motion bulk averages hide.
scenes.caption: On its track, each motor foot grips, swings while gripping, lets go, and re-cocks. One step's work cannot exceed the energy of one ATP. Force times step is at most about 80 to 100 pN·nm. Watching purified parts one by one reveals motion bulk averages hide.
scenes.visual: Zoom slightly within the same glass chamber onto one simple two-footed motor schematic on a polar track. Synchronize the foot animation with each narrated beat: grip the track, swing forward while gripping, release, and re-cock as one ATP dot flashes. Above the track, write the clean formula 'force x step <= 80-100 pN·nm' (computed limit from given numbers; motor and track labelled schematic) as a gauge bar fills up to the ceiling without crossing it. Subtle drifting specks keep ambient motion alive.
scenes.narration: On its track, each motor foot grips, swings while gripping, lets go, and re-cocks. One step's work cannot exceed the energy of one ATP. Force times step is at most about 80 to 100 pN·nm. Watching purified parts one by one reveals motion bulk averages hide.

scenes.tts: If one foot always grips, one kinesin one or myosin five walks alone. Muscle myosin two also has two heads. In our chamber, could one myosin two molecule carry a vesicle along actin?
scenes.caption: If one foot always grips, one kinesin-1 or myosin V walks alone. Muscle myosin II also has two heads. In our chamber, could one myosin II molecule carry a vesicle along actin?
scenes.visual: Same glass chamber (schematic). First, a single two-footed walker labelled 'Kinesin-1 / Myosin V' steps steadily along a polar track with one foot always touching. It fades aside as a single two-headed schematic motor labelled 'Myosin II' appears above a glowing actin filament holding a simple round vesicle. As the question is asked, show the short prompt 'Can one myosin II walk?' at top.
scenes.narration: If one foot always grips, one kinesin-1 or myosin V walks alone. Muscle myosin II also has two heads. In our chamber, could one myosin II molecule carry a vesicle along actin?

scenes.visual: Hold the same glass chamber with the single two-headed myosin II schematic holding its vesicle right above the glowing actin filament, and the prompt 'Can one myosin II walk?' still on screen. Keep slow ambient shimmer in the fluid and gentle bobbing of the vesicle so the frame is alive during the thinking pause.

scenes.tts: No: myosin two feet spend most of each cycle off the track. A lone molecule would drift off, so muscle myosin two works in a crowd. Purified-motor tests also catch direction exceptions. Purified myosin six moves toward actin's pointed end. Fruit-fly kinesin n c d moves toward the microtubule minus end.
scenes.caption: No: myosin II feet spend most of each cycle off the track. A lone molecule would drift off, so muscle myosin II works in a crowd. Purified-motor tests also catch direction exceptions. Purified myosin VI moves toward actin's pointed end. Fruit-fly kinesin ncd moves toward the microtubule minus end.
scenes.visual: Same glass chamber (schematic). The lone myosin II grips briefly, then both feet release and the motor plus vesicle drift away from actin. Several more myosin II motors enter along the glass floor as a crowd and smoothly slide the glowing actin filament forward. Then two clean tracks side by side inside the chamber show direction reversals: a glowing arrow moves 'Myosin VI' toward actin's pointed (-) end, and 'ncd' moves toward the microtubule's minus (-) end.
scenes.narration: No: myosin II feet spend most of each cycle off the track. A lone molecule would drift off, so muscle myosin II works in a crowd. Purified-motor tests also catch direction exceptions. Purified myosin VI moves toward actin's pointed end. Fruit-fly kinesin ncd moves toward the microtubule minus end.

scenes.tts: Still, glowing spots under a microscope can mislead. Clusters below the microscope's resolution look round, just like liquid droplets. Drifting clusters look merged unless they relax into one round body. Bleaching fluorescence and watching glow return, called F R A P, measures turnover that binding and unbinding also give.
scenes.caption: Still, glowing spots under a microscope can mislead. Clusters below the microscope's resolution look round, just like liquid droplets. Drifting clusters look merged unless they relax into one round body. Bleaching fluorescence and watching glow return, called FRAP, measures turnover that binding and unbinding also give.
scenes.visual: Stay in the dark microscope field of view (all schematic). Two blurry round glowing spots sit side by side: one resolves into a tight irregular cluster of dots while the other is a soft droplet, showing why resolution hides the difference. Two clusters drift together without smoothing out, contrasted with two droplets merging and relaxing into one round body. Then a bright laser flash bleaches a circular spot dark (label 'FRAP'), and fresh glowing dots bind and unbind to refill the glow.
scenes.narration: Still, glowing spots under a microscope can mislead. Clusters below the microscope's resolution look round, just like liquid droplets. Drifting clusters look merged unless they relax into one round body. Bleaching fluorescence and watching glow return, called FRAP, measures turnover that binding and unbinding also give.

scenes.tts: Bleaching half a large spot tests whether molecules mix inside it faster than they cross its edge. Faster inside mixing favours a liquid droplet without proving one. Motor chambers have their own limit. A chamber result describes motors outside the cell, at low load unless a load is stated.
scenes.caption: Bleaching half a large spot tests whether molecules mix inside it faster than they cross its edge. Faster inside mixing favours a liquid droplet without proving one. Motor chambers have their own limit. A chamber result describes motors outside the cell, at low load unless a load is stated.
scenes.visual: Same microscope view (schematic). A large glowing round spot has only its right half bleached dark (label 'Half-body FRAP'); bright dots shuffle across the middle faster than across the outer rim, while a small hedge tag reads 'Favours, not proof'. Pull back to our glass chamber: show an isolated motor stepping on a free track with a small label 'Outside the cell, low load' (schematic).
scenes.narration: Bleaching half a large spot tests whether molecules mix inside it faster than they cross its edge. Faster inside mixing favours a liquid droplet without proving one. scenes.tts: With those guards, microscope chambers unlocked three breakthroughs. Summers and Gibbons briefly treated sea-urchin sperm axonemes, the cores of their tails, with the protein-cutting enzyme trypsin. It disrupted what resists sliding. With zero point one millimolar A T P under dark-field microscopy, groups of microtubule doublets slid out. So dynein slides microtubules rather than shortening them.
scenes.caption: With those guards, microscope chambers unlocked three breakthroughs. Summers and Gibbons briefly treated sea-urchin sperm axonemes, the cores of their tails, with the protein-cutting enzyme trypsin. It disrupted what resists sliding. With 0.1 mM ATP under dark-field microscopy, groups of microtubule doublets slid out. So dynein slides microtubules rather than shortening them.
scenes.visual: Return to our dark glass microscope chamber in dark-field style (bright outlines on dark fluid, schematic). A bundled sea-urchin sperm axoneme of parallel microtubule doublets sits intact with cross-links resisting motion. Small scissor icons labelled 'Trypsin' snip the cross-links. When glowing dots labelled '0.1 mM ATP' enter, groups of bright doublets telescope and slide outward from the bundle without shrinking in length; label 'Summers & Gibbons'.
scenes.narration: With those guards, microscope chambers unlocked three breakthroughs. Summers and Gibbons briefly treated sea-urchin sperm axonemes, the cores of their tails, with the protein-cutting enzyme trypsin. It disrupted what resists sliding. With 0.1 mM ATP under dark-field microscopy, groups of microtubule doublets slid out. So dynein slides microtubules rather than shortening them.

scenes.tts: Second, in nineteen eighty-four, Mitchison and Kirschner inferred dynamic instability from microtubule populations. Their ends switch between steady growth and rapid shortening. Microscopy of single purified ends soon showed those switches directly.
scenes.caption: Second, in 1984, Mitchison and Kirschner inferred dynamic instability from microtubule populations. Their ends switch between steady growth and rapid shortening. Microscopy of single purified ends soon showed those switches directly.
scenes.visual: Same dark glass chamber (schematic). A faint crowd of many microtubules fades away into one bright purified microtubule filling the frame horizontally. Label 'Mitchison & Kirschner, 1984' briefly appears. The microtubule's end extends steadily subunit by subunit, abruptly switches to rapid peeling contraction, then pauses and grows steadily again, matching the narrated switches.
scenes.narration: Second, in 1984, Mitchison and Kirschner inferred dynamic instability from microtubule populations. Their ends switch between steady growth and rapid shortening. Microscopy of single purified ends soon showed those switches directly.

scenes.tts: Third, Noji and Yoshida fixed A T P synthase heads to glass with a fluorescent actin filament. The heads spun the filament in discrete one hundred twenty degree steps, one per A T P. Isolated on glass, single parts show what the crowd's average hides.
scenes.caption: Third, Noji and Yoshida fixed ATP synthase heads to glass with a fluorescent actin filament. The heads spun the filament in discrete 120° steps, one per ATP. Isolated on glass, single parts show what the crowd's average hides.
scenes.visual: Same glass chamber, viewed from above looking down at the glass floor. A simple motor base labelled 'ATP synthase' sits fixed to the glass with a long bright fluorescent actin rod attached like a compass needle (schematic structure; rotation angle computed at exact 120° increments). Each time an ATP dot flashes, the glowing actin rod snaps cleanly through 120° and pauses, tracing three positions around a circle; label 'Noji & Yoshida'. As the closing lines play, the glowing rod continues gentle 120° steps while the chamber edges glow softly and a faint blurred crowd of motors fades out behind it.
scenes.narration: Third, Noji and Yoshida fixed ATP synthase heads to glass with a fluorescent actin filament. The heads spun the filament in discrete 120° steps, one per ATP. Isolated on glass, single parts show what the crowd's average hides.

scenes.visual: Clean dark end card matching the chamber background, with subtle slow drifting light specks and the centered take-home rule in high-contrast text: 'Watch purified parts under a microscope to see what averages hide.'
